name: LT6106IS5#TRMPBF
title: LT6106: 36 V high-side current sense amplifier in TSOT-23
summary: A high-side current sense amplifier that converts the drop across an external shunt into an output current set by one resistor, RIN; a second resistor, ROUT, turns that current into a ground-referred voltage, so two resistors set the gain. It runs from 2.7 V to 36 V (44 V absolute maximum) on 65 µA typical, with 250 µV maximum offset and 40 nA maximum input bias current. LT6106IS5#TRMPBF is the –40 °C to 85 °C grade on a 500-unit reel.
key_figures: 2.7 V to 36 V; 44 V absolute maximum

pins.name: OUT
pins.function: Current output. The current it sources into an external resistor follows the sense voltage in proportion.

pins.name: –IN
pins.function: Inverting input. The amplifier forces it to the voltage of +IN; RIN from V+ to this pin sets IOUT = VSENSE/RIN, where VSENSE is the drop across RSENSE.

pins.name: +IN
pins.function: Non-inverting input. Connects to the load end of the shunt, directly or through a resistor.

pins.name: V+
pins.function: Positive supply, connected straight to one end of RSENSE; the part's supply current flows in this pin. On the supply end of the shunt only the load current is measured; on the load end the part's own current is measured too.

tables.title: Absolute maximum ratings
notes: Note 1: Operating beyond these ratings can damage the part for good, and holding it at any of them for long spells can shorten its life. The output current also has to be kept low enough that the die stays at or below 150°C.

Note 4: LT6106C is guaranteed to work from –40°C to 85°C and is designed and characterised to meet its specifications over that span, though it is neither tested nor QA sampled there. LT6106I is guaranteed to meet its specifications from –40°C to 85°C, and LT6106H from –40°C to 125°C.

circuits.title: 3 V to 36 V, 5 A current sense with AV = 10
circuits.description: A 0.02 Ω shunt in the supply line to the load turns 5 A into 100 mV. RIN = 100 Ω and ROUT = 1k give a voltage gain of 10, so the ground-referred output reads 200 mV per amp. V+ and the top of RIN both tie to the supply end of the shunt; +IN takes the load end.

circuits.title: Kelvin input connection (Figure 2)
circuits.description: The basic hookup, with RIN and +IN taken straight from the two sense terminals of the shunt so that copper carrying the load current adds no error to the measured voltage. V+ ties to the supply end of the shunt.

circuits.title: Shunt diode limits the sense voltage (Figure 3)
circuits.description: A Schottky diode across the shunt clamps the sense voltage at large currents. This lets RIN be smaller than the 1 mA output limit would otherwise allow, giving finer resolution at small currents while large currents read low.

circuits.title: Second input resistor for bias-current error (Figure 4)
circuits.description: A resistor RIN+ between the load end of the shunt and +IN, chosen as RIN– minus RSENSE, balances the source resistance the two inputs see so that the bias currents cancel and only the offset current remains as an error.

circuits.title: Supply current monitored with the load (Figure 5)
circuits.description: V+ takes its supply from the load end of the shunt, so the part's own supply current passes through RSENSE and is counted along with the load current. +IN, –IN and V+ then sit at the same voltage.

circuits.title: Schottky diode against supply reversal (Figure 6)
circuits.description: A Schottky diode D1 in series between V– and ground blocks current through the part if the battery is connected backwards. It costs one diode drop of supply headroom in normal use.

circuits.title: Output resistor against supply reversal (Figure 7)
circuits.description: The reverse-diode circuit with its output feeding an ADC. R3 (1k) between OUT and the ADC input limits the current if the ADC's input clamp would hold the output at a high voltage while the supply is reversed.

circuits.title: Simple 400 V current monitor
circuits.description: The part floats on a 400 V supply: a 12 V zener from the rail sets the part's own supply, and a BAT46 with P-channel MOSFET M2 and a 2M resistor hold its V– node. P-channel MOSFET M1, gated from V–, passes the output current down to a ground-referred ROUT of 4.99k, giving VOUT = 49.9 × VSENSE with RIN = 100 Ω. Lethal voltages are present on this circuit.

operation.text: An internal amplifier loop holds –IN at the same voltage as +IN. With RIN from V+ to –IN, the sense voltage appears across RIN and a current VSENSE/RIN flows in it. The amplifier inputs take almost none of that current, so it passes through an internal PNP transistor and leaves at OUT as IOUT. A resistor from OUT to V– turns it into a ground-referred voltage.

The upper bound on RSENSE comes from the largest sense voltage allowed at peak load, and its dissipation; the lower bound from the smallest current to be resolved against the 150 µV typical input offset. Example: a 100 mV maximum at 2 A peak needs RSENSE ≤ 50 mΩ; then the offset equals 3 mA of load current and peak shunt dissipation is 200 mW. A 5 mΩ shunt cuts the peak sense voltage to 10 mV at 2 A and the dissipation to 20 mW, but the offset then equals 30 mA. A 20 mA minimum current into 7.5 mΩ gives 150 µV, equal to the offset. The 150 µV typical offset gives 60 dB of dynamic range at 150 mV full scale and over 70 dB at 0.5 V.

Take –IN and +IN to the shunt by Kelvin connections except at the lowest powers. A 10 mm × 10 mm square of 1 oz copper is about 0.5 mΩ, so 2 A in it makes 1 mV, a 1% error on a 100 mV signal; 10 A makes 5%. A shunt with its own Kelvin sense terminals is best (Figure 2).

RIN is at most 500 Ω, and should keep IOUT at or below 1 mA at the largest sense voltage expected; choosing it so that this sense voltage gives exactly 1 mA uses the full output range. A larger RIN lowers the output current and dissipation when less range is needed. A smaller RIN may be used if something else limits the current, such as a Schottky diode across RSENSE (Figure 3), trading high-current accuracy for low-current resolution. Trace and interconnect resistance adds to RIN and shows up as gain error, which matters most for small RIN.

VOUT = IOUT × ROUT, so ROUT sets the output range: IOUT(MAX) × ROUT should stay within the input range of the buffer or ADC that follows. ROUT is also the output impedance; a driven stage with low input resistance, or one that draws current spikes as an ADC does, may need a smaller ROUT. A driven input resistance of 100 × ROUT costs 1% of accuracy.

Resistor mismatch gives a gain error only. Input offset voltage adds directly to VSENSE and is the main error, setting the bottom of the dynamic range. Typical gain error is –0.25% at 1 mA output, mostly from the finite gain of the output PNP: a small part of the RIN current does not reach ROUT.

At VSENSE = 0 V the output is always a little above zero, from the input offset and from 0.7 µA to 1.2 µA of quiescent current through the output device. The specified minimum output voltage includes both.

The output delivers at least 1 mA and can deliver more depending on conditions. Keep the maximum output current within limits through the choice of RSENSE and RIN, and with external clamps where input faults can occur.

VOUT = IOUT × ZOUT, so any network giving the wanted ZOUT filters the output. A capacitor across ROUT makes a lowpass, cutting noise, and also serves as a charge reservoir that holds the output steady when it drives a switched load such as a MUX or ADC.

Connect V+ to either end of the shunt; both satisfy +IN ≤ V+ and –IN ≤ V+. In normal operation VSENSE stays at or below 500 mV, that is V+ – (+IN) ≤ 500 mV. The loop drives +IN and –IN to VS – VSENSE. With V+ on the supply end, the inputs sit VSENSE below V+ and the part's supply current is not measured; with V+ on the load end (Figure 5), all three pins are at the same voltage and the supply current is measured with the load. In both cases the output current is not measured, since it is drawn through RIN from the supply side of the shunt. Operation with V+ outside the recommended range is a matter for the factory.

The part has no internal protection against a reversed supply. A Schottky diode in series with V– (Figure 6) limits the reverse current, at the cost of reducing the part's supply by the diode drop VD. If the output connects to something that would clamp it to a high voltage during reversal, such as an ESD clamp, add a series resistor or Schottky diode at the output (Figure 7).
When the output current is very low or zero and the input steps, the output starts to move only after a delay while internal nodes charge.
Demo board DC1240 carries the LT6106.

All grades carry the same marking, LTCWK; the temperature grade is shown on a label on the shipping container. #TRMPBF parts come on 500-unit reels. Only the #W parts are the automotive grade, made under controlled manufacturing for automotive use.
